title: Meeting Armstrong and proving he could read music
summary: Randolph took a tune to Armstrong at the Regal, and Armstrong sang the difficult intervals at sight, convincing Randolph that the rumor he could not read was false.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: I see. Well, when did you first meet Louie? You started to tell me that. You were teaching Lil arranging I think you said.

I was teaching Lil. I met Louie when he came back to do a show at the Regal, and I went back and carried a tune that I had written. The title of my tune then was -- I'll think of it -- da-da-da-da-- 'I Don't Care What You
Do, or something like that. But anyway, I didn't know too much about Louie and everybody had told me that Louie couldn't read music. Did you ever hear that?
Yeah. Well, that's what was kicked around. They said Louie couldn't read music.

Well, now, I can't -- I carried this tune to Louie and Louie sat down and so here's what happened. When Louie took this tune and looked at it, Louie started singing it -- da-da-da-da-- then I began to look as though I had seen a ghost or something because it just took me off my feet. And the intervals that I had in there -- da-da-da-da-

He was singing all those intervals and doing this way in the chair, he was singing the intervals, and he said to me, "Randy, that's pretty. That's really a pretty tune." But we never did get a chance to record it, though. But -- and I knew right then, I went back and told my wife, I said, "They say Louie can't read music. Louie took that song and solfeged that song off." (unintelligible)? See, that's the solfeggio. I said, "He solfeged that song off direct from sight -- sight reading." And so, then I knew he could read. Then after -- when I started arranging for him, the parts that I would pick for him -- his parts out -- I knew he could read then.
You did write parts for him?
Oh, yeah. I wrote parts for Louie. Yes. I wrote parts.
